name: Femur
description: Distal femur: medial and lateral condyles, joined anteriorly by the trochlea and separated posteriorly by the intercondylar notch. In adults the epiphyseal marrow is fatty (bright on T1, dark on fat-sat), the metaphysis may hold patchy red marrow, and a thin smooth line often marks the closed physis. Sagittal images show the condyles and notch, axial images the trochlea, coronal images the weight-bearing surfaces.

normal_values.trochlear_depth: more than 3 mm on axial, 3 cm above the femorotibial joint line; 3 mm or less indicates trochlear dysplasia (Pfirrmann 2000: sensitivity 100%, specificity 96%)
normal_values.lateral_trochlear_inclination: 11° or more on the most proximal axial image showing trochlear cartilage, against the posterior condylar line; below 11° indicates dysplasia (Carrillon 2000: sensitivity 93%, specificity 87%)
normal_values.trochlear_facet_ratio: medial to lateral facet length 2:5 (40%) or more on axial, 3 cm above the joint line; lower indicates dysplasia (Pfirrmann 2000)
normal_values.lateral_femoral_notch_depth: 1.5 mm or less at the condylopatellar sulcus on sagittal; deeper supports ACL tear (Gentili 1994: specificity 100%, sensitivity 19%)

variants_pitfalls: Red marrow in the distal metaphysis is common: over half of women and under a sixth of men (most often women aged 30–60, also obesity and smoking; Wilson 1996), and 43% of marathon runners (Shellock 1992). It is patchy or flame-shaped, isointense to or brighter than muscle on T1 and spares the epiphysis; marrow darker than muscle on T1, epiphyseal extension or cortical breach needs workup.

Physeal scar: a thin, smooth, transverse low-signal line across the full width of the former physis persists into adulthood and is not a fracture (no edema, no step). In adolescents with a narrowed, closing physis, a focal central edema zone straddling it (FOPE, 2–27 mm, ages about 12–16) is physiologic (Zbojniewicz 2011).

Posteromedial distal femoral cortical irregularity (cortical desmoid): a saucer-shaped cortical defect, T1 low and T2 high with a dark rim, at the medial gastrocnemius attachment (about 93–95%) or adductor magnus, often bilateral. Seen on 9–27% of adolescent knee MRIs and 58% of youth alpine skiers (Gaukroger 2025; Stern 2020); a do-not-touch lesion, not for biopsy.

Irregular ossification of the posterior condyles in children (22% of children; peak ages 2–12 in boys, 2–10 in girls; 99.6% posterior; Jans 2011) mimics OCD. Favor a variant when it is posterior, the overlying cartilage is intact, there are accessory ossicles or spiculation and no marrow edema (Gebarski 2005).
